title: Benedict and Scholastica (6th century)
hookLine: twin brother and sister; she prays for a storm so he'll stay and talk

lines: A STORM FROM A CLEAR SKY.
cards: Italy, the five hundreds. Benedict runs a monastery on a mountain called Monte Cassino. His sister Scholastica leads a community of women not far away; tradition says they were twins.
Once a year they meet at a little house halfway between, and spend the day talking about God. One year it gets dark, and she asks him to stay the night so they can keep talking. He says no.
Absolutely not: his own rule says a monk sleeps in the monastery. So Scholastica folds her hands on the table, puts her head down on them, and prays.
And out of a clear evening sky comes a storm so violent that nobody can set foot outside.

teach.h: I ASKED MY GOD, AND HE LISTENED.
teach.b: The story comes from Pope Gregory the Great, who wrote Benedict's life about fifty years after he died. Benedict, stuck, says something like: God forgive you, sister, what have you done?
And she answers: I asked you, and you wouldn't listen. So I asked my God, and he listened. Now go, if you can.
They talk all night. Three days later Scholastica dies, and Benedict buries her in the tomb he'd prepared for himself.

teach.h: SHE COULD DO MORE: SHE LOVED MORE.
teach.b: Gregory adds a line people still quote: she could do more, because she loved more.
Benedict wrote one of the most important books in Western history: a short Rule for monks.

It opens with one word, listen, and it arranges a whole day around prayer, work and reading, in balance, so no one is crushed and no one is idle. Monks and nuns still live by it, fifteen centuries later.
For a thousand years, Benedictine monasteries kept books, farms, schools and hospitality alive across Europe; the Rule says every guest should be welcomed as Christ himself.
The motto people give it is pray and work, in Latin ora et labora. Those exact words aren't in the Rule. They're a later summary, but a good one.
And the storm is the perfect footnote: even the man who wrote the rule had to learn from his sister that love can outrank a schedule.

how: Benedictine monks and nuns live by the Rule of Saint Benedict, praying the hours together and working in between; Catholics keep Scholastica's feast on 10 February and Benedict's on 11 July.

o: the prayer Scholastica said to bring the storm
the first word of Benedict's Rule for monks
a monk's vow to keep silent through the day

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.

s: ora et labora is written in Benedict's Rule
the words aren't in the Rule. they're a later summary of it.
Benedict buried Scholastica in his own tomb
Gregory says he laid her in the tomb he'd prepared for himself.
Benedict happily agreed to stay the night
he refused. then the storm came.

games.q: you're Benedict. it's getting dark, and your sister begs you to stay and keep talking. your own rule says a monk sleeps in the monastery. what do you do?
o: refuse, and get ready to leave.
take her back to the monastery.
games.why: he refuses. she bows her head and prays, a storm breaks from a clear sky, and he can't leave. they talk all night.

practice: Think of someone you always talk to in a rush, between meetings, in the car, half-looking at a screen, and picture sitting down with them with nowhere else to be, like Scholastica at that table.
What would you ask, and what would you finally have time to hear? If you pray, you can pray for that person, and for time.

wordCard.voice: listen. The first word of Benedict's Rule for monks, which balanced prayer, work and reading across the whole day.

orig.note: Latin: pray and work. a later motto summing up Benedict's Rule.

carryVoice: Your line: pray and work. Prayer, work and reading, each in its place. Day eighty-seven, done.

sources.ref: Rule of Saint Benedict, Prologue; chapters 48, 53
